Title: Does the Game Win rule cloud the objective?

Messages.Author: Chris Arthur
Messages.Body:
I was a judge at the recent Australian Nationals and I would like to
share my thoughts regarding the direction of playstyle and see if
anyone here has similar thoughts. Up until the Game Win rule was
introduced it seemed that tournament decks were very forward focussed
because making the final was simply a matter of the number of vp's
accrued. Nowadays, and particularly at our recent championships, a
large number of decks are either defensive in construction or played
defensively. Withdraw deals also seem to be flavour of the month (four
out of seven tables in the first round). It seems that players are
happy to simply get a game win and are not building decks that can
sweep or going all out to sweep. I am not suggesting that they were
not playing to maximise their vps however i am suggesting that the
mental calculations people use to decide whether to take a hassle-free
3 vps over a more difficult 4 vps are influenced by the Game Win rule.

I have noticed that several posters in the past have posted things
like:

1) A player must try to obtain the game win.
2) If a player has no reasonable chance of a game win, he must try to
maximize his VPs.
3) If the player has no reasonable chance of getting more than zero
VPs (or he has already obtained the game win), he may play however he
wants (including self-ousting, giving away VPs, etc.)

and this seems to support the idea that obtaining a game win has a
higher priority than maximising vps however i could find no basis for
the above priority list in the online rules (rulebook and tournament).
All I found was the object of the game from the rulebook:

"Your goal is to accumulate the most victory points"

and this from the tournament rules:

"Players must not play toward goals that conflict with the goal of the
game as stated in the V:TES rulebook"

I myself recently agreed to a withdraw deal that gave me 3 vps where i
was in a position where i had a roughly 15% chance to get 3.5vps and
about a 5% chance to get 5 vps. Should i have gone for the 3.5 vps (or
5)? The fact that the virtually guaranteed 3vps gave me the game win
influenced my decision. If a game win was defined as 3.5 vps (for
whatever reason) i doubt that i would have gone for the withdraw deal.
Is it ok to have your decisions influenced by the Game Win rule or
should you always be gunning for the most vps even if it would
jeopardise your chances of getting a game win?

Chris.

p.s. Having said all that the Aussie championships where won by a very
forward focussed deck.

I apologise for the following nitpick but it's only as a judge that
i've come to think that the goals of the game have not really been
clearly defined. There were a lot of players at the Australian
Championships who believed that the goal was to maximise your vps.
These are long term players so unless its an Australian aberration
perhaps the problem lies in the rules?

nitpick:
As stated in the rulebook:

"Your goal is to accumulate the most victory points"

The winner of a game according to the rulebook:
"At the end of the game, the winner is the player with the most
victory points"

In the tournament rules there is no rule that says you have to play to
win. The only mention i could find was in the rules for
Unsportsmanlike conduct:

"Players must not play toward goals that conflict with the goal of the
game as stated in the V:TES rulebook"

The goal in the rulebook however only talks about getting the most vps
so is it possible to play for 1.5vps (with everyone else on less)?
Even if you could theoretically get more? If not then is there an
implicit assumption that the player is playing to win? If so why the
line in the Unsportsmanlike Conduct section? Why not just state the
goals explicitly?

Chris.

No. GWs are a tournament-based ranking construct (number of such
Game Wins, where not all instances of winning the game count as Game
Wins).

Even if it were, that would not validate your original assertion:

"That goal is to score the most VPs; NOT to win the game."

Since scoring 1.5-1.0-1.0-1.0-0.0 is scoring the most VPs (and,
therefore, winning the game) while not getting a tournament GW.

Every instance of achieving a GW is an instance of winning the game
and, therefore, of getting the most VPs, since the latter two are
one and the same.
